endorsements.quote: High-risk tools may undergo silent deployment, running in the live electronic health record with hidden outputs, to observe performance before exposing clinicians, while lower-risk pilots can use shorter silent trials to gather telemetry without disrupting care.

Each stage serves as a sequential gate; failure to meet criteria halts advancement until deficiencies are addressed and criteria are met, and culminates in a structured report to support transparent, accountable decision-making regarding AI adoption in emergency care.

Emergency physicians must test vendor claims by mapping the exact workflow step where recommendations surface and judging whether those outputs are actionable amid real-world constraints, including staffing ratios, wait times, CT queues, boarding, and alert fatigue.
Financial analysis is performed to ensure the AI tool represents a sustainable investment, factoring in all pertinent expenditures related to building or purchasing the solution.

Departmental leaders need to take into consideration the perspective of diverse stakeholders, including fellow physicians, nurses, patients, underrepresented communities, and technical staff, with the goal of identifying potential ethical conflicts or oversights in model design and deployment.
Clinicians need to be able to identify potential conflicts of interests and signs of algorithmic bias that could exacerbate health disparities for vulnerable populations.

For nongenerative AI, single purpose tools such as clinical decision support and predictive algorithms should be classified as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) when applicable, with clear intended use cases, representative training data, and Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCP) for safe updates and monitoring across the entire product lifecycle.

During this phase, emergency physicians become clinical champions, utilizing implementation science best practices, and convening with nurses and ancillary staff to codesign workflows that account for operational hurdles.
These champions provide practical tip sheets and reference guides to standardize use and minimize cognitive burden.
The Educate pillar aims to establish a shared foundation of AI literacy across the emergency medicine workforce.
Successful implementation requires physicians be ready to apply the framework by leveraging a shared online hub with training materials and foundational content on AI in medicine.

unlisted_practices: Establish a national Emergency Medicine AI Advisory Council to issue shared terminology, nonbinding best-practice guidance, and implementation toolkits.

Standardize AI education from residency through continuing medical education using specialty-specific competencies, embedding algorithm appraisal, bias mitigation, and data governance into residency milestones and CME requirements.
Assess prospective AI vendors' clinical credibility, track record, financial stability, and market traction through due diligence before partnership.
Have large well-resourced institutions openly share AI curricula, implementation guides, and evaluation tools.
Establish core AI competencies for certification and accreditation of emergency physicians.
Hold daily debrief sessions after go-live to recalibrate the AI tool and associated workflow.
Provide on-site clinical champions for troubleshooting and coaching during initial AI deployment.
Include physicians on AI development teams and involve clinicians in AI tool design.

screen.reason: Expert consensus opinion and policy recommendations from the ACEP AI Task Force on AI education, evaluation frameworks, and governance in emergency medicine.
